title: Naval on wealth as knowledge: Deutsch's definition, ethical wealth creation, and hard-to-vary products
summary: Naval revisits his "assets that earn while you sleep" definition of wealth through David Deutsch's lens: wealth is the set of physical transformations you can effect, and knowledge, not capital, is the multiplier. He argues ethical wealth creation is possible and cynicism is self-defeating. He then applies Deutsch to products: good ones are hard to vary, and technology markets carry network effects and scale economies.

principles.text: Wealth is assets that earn while you sleep, so you escape the input-tied-to-output trap.
principles.quote: my definition of wealth was assets that earn while you sleep.

principles.text: Deutsch's deeper view: knowledge, not capital, is the big multiplier of wealth.
principles.quote: If you pay careful attention, you realize that knowledge is the big multiplier. It's not the capital.

principles.text: Believe ethical wealth creation is possible. Cynicism is self-fulfilling and keeps you stuck.
principles.quote: cynics, their beliefs are self-fulfilling. You will be stuck in the mud.

principles.text: The most ethical move is to take risk yourself and bear its consequences (skin in the game).
principles.quote: the most ethical thing you can do is be a risk taker. you be an entrepreneur, you go and you bear risk.

principles.text: Good products are hard to vary. Selling multiple versions needs a really good reason.
principles.quote: if you're selling multiple versions of your product, you better have a really good reason for that.

principles.text: All technology has network effects and scale economies, so the best product wins by amortizing R&D over the largest base.
principles.quote: all of technology has network effects and has scale economies.
